Kamlet–Taft Parameters of Deep Eutectic Solvents and Their Relationship with Dissolution of Main Lignocellulosic Components
Luyao Zhang,§ Haitao Yu,§ Shuo Liu, Yang Wang, Tiancheng Mu, and Zhimin Xue*
Cite This: Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2023, 62, 11723–11734 --- Read Online
ACCESS | Metrics & More | Article Recommendations | SI Supporting Information

ABSTRACT: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted significant interest in dissolving lignocellulosic components. However, revealing the relationship between the solvation properties of DESs and their ability to dissolve lignocellulosic components remains a significant challenge. Herein, 56 DESs were prepared and applied to dissolve lignocellulosic components. This revealed that the Kamlet–Taft parameters (i.e., α, β, and π*) were significantly affected by the structures of DESs. More notably, the correlation between Kamlet–Taft parameters and solubility varied with DESs and lignocellulosic components. Concretely, DESs have greater values of β and β−α (net basicity), are expected to dissolve cellulose efficiently, have greater net basicity, and are favorable to dissolve lignin, and the solubility of xylan was linearly correlated with the β value. # 1. INTRODUCTION Lignocellulose, composed of three primary lignocellulosic components of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, is the largest renewable resource on earth. It can be used as an abundantly available raw material to produce value-added products, including transportation fuels, platform chemicals, and functional materials. 1,2 Generally, dissolution is indis- pensable to the efficient utilization or conversion of lignocellulose. Significant effort has been devoted to developing suitable solvents to dissolve lignocellulosic components, a research hotspot in the field of lignocellulose.3 Of the developed solvent systems, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been recognized as an emerging class of functional solvents for the dissolution of lignocellulosic components. Generally, DESs are composed of two components via the hydrogen bonding interaction to generate a eutectic mixture, and the two components are hydrogen- bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA), respectively. 4,5 The DESs designed by selecting suitable HBDs and HBAs of different properties could enable them to possess various unique advantages, e.g., strong solvation ability, good designability, low cost, facile preparation, high biocompati- bility, etc. 4-8 These characteristics of DESs promote the continually growing interest in constructing efficient DESs to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, or lignin.9-12 As reported, DESs can be defined as the mixture of two or more pure compounds with a eutectic point temperature below that for an ideal liquid mixture, showing significantly negative deviations from ideality. 13 More importantly, the composition of DESs

should be in a certain range, not just in a fixed stoichiometric proportion. 13 Based on this definition, all the prepared solvents in this work can be considered as DESs. Regarding the utilization of DESs in lignocellulosic chemistry, the current attention is mainly focused on designing novel DESs for the pretreatment of lignocellulose or dissolution of the three major components. 14 Very little attention has been paid to system- atically analyze the relationship between the properties of DESs and the dissolution of lignocellulosic components, resulting in limited rules that can be followed to design or screen suitable DESs to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. 15

As is well known, whether a DES is a good solvent or not is mostly related to its solvation ability. Generally, the solvation properties of one specific solvent can be evaluated by Kamlet- Taft solvatochromic parameters (i.e., α, β, and π*), in which α represents the hydrogen-bond-donating ability (i.e., Lewis acidity), β represents the hydrogen-bond-accepting ability (i.e., Lewis basicity), and π* represents the polarizability of the solvents. Hong et al. found that a lower lignin yield was achieved from the pretreatment of poplar in choline chloride/ oxalic acid (ChCl/OA) than ChCl/lactic acid (ChCl/LA),¹⁷ probably resulting from the higher α-β value of ChCl/OA (1.10) than that of ChCl/LA (0.80). Liang et al. utilized 10 types of LA-based DESs to pretreat corn straw¹⁸ and observed a positive correlation between α and the pretreatment performance. Moreover, a positive linear relationship between α and the extraction efficiency of lignin was found when using different ChCl-based DESs to pretreat pine wood.¹⁹ In addition, our previous works showed that the solubility of lignin had a positive correlation with α and π* of the DESs, while the solubility of xylan had a positive correlation with β.¹¹,²⁰

However, previous works only investigated the relationship between Kamlet–Taft parameters of limited types of DESs and their performance on the pretreatment/dissolution of lignocellulose. More difficultly, although Kamlet–Taft parameters of some DESs have been experimentally determined or theoretically predicted,²¹ the reported parameters of DES are still highly limited compared with the great amount of DESs, let alone to numerous possible combinations of DESs which have not been investigated.²² Besides, the parameters reported in different works were not obtained by compatible methods, leading to the incomparability of these parameters. Owing to

the insufficient and even incompatible data, Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters were still not the good indicators on the solute solubility in comparison with the surface tension and pKₐ. Therefore, it is a great challenge to evaluate the performance of DES on the dissolution of lignocellulosic components using the Kamlet–Taft parameters.²³ More effort should be devoted on investigating the correlation between the structures of DESs and Kamlet–Taft parameters and the relationship between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the solubility of lignocellulosic components.

To better understand the Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs to facilitate the design of DESs to dissolve lignocellulosic components, 56 kinds of DESs were prepared using different HBAs and HBDs. Emphasizing, these DESs were selected based on the properties of HBAs and HBDs. Some previously reported DESs were directly selected, and most of the involved DESs were prepared based on our continuous jobs on the preparation of novel DESs to dissolve the lignocellulosic components. Initially, the influence of the structure (chain length) and properties of HBDs and HBAs on Kamlet–Taft parameters was analyzed. Additionally, the Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs were compared with those of conventional solvents and ionic liquids (ILs), providing a macroscopic image of Kamlet–Taft parameters of different solvents. ## 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals used for the preparation of DESs were obtained from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd (Beijing, China), Energy Chemical (Beijing, China), J&K Scientific, Fluorochem (Old Glossop, U.K.), Acros Organic, and Sigma-Aldrich (Shanghai, China), separately. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters for DESs and the solubility of lignin/xylan/cellulose in DESs were determined according to our previous work. 10 The Kamlet-Taft linear solvation energy relationship (LSER) method was used to determine the correlation between solubility and Kamlet-Taft parameters. 24,25 The detailed procedures are provided in the Supporting Information section.

## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ### 3.1. Measurement of Kamlet–Taft Solvatochromic Parameters of DESs. The Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of the involved DESs (56 kinds, Scheme 1) were determined by the maximum UV–vis absorption peaks of the solutions of three dyes (Figure S1). The corresponding Kamlet–Taft parameters was the average of twice the measurements for each DES obtained from twice preparations (Table S2). Herein, it was emphasized that the Kamlet–Taft parameters of different solvents were determined using the same dyes (i.e., _N,N_-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4-nitroaniline, and Nile red) to exclude the influence of different dyes on the values of Kamlet–Taft parameters and make the results be comparable. By analyzing the values of α, β, and π*, we could conclude the relationship between the values of Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters and the structures and properties of DESs. Furthermore, by combining the solubility of cellulose, lignin, and hemicellulose in DESs, the correlation between solubility and Kamlet–Taft parameters could be revealed to some extent.

3.2. Influence of DESs' Structures on the Kamlet–Taft Solvatochromic Parameters. 3.2.1. Effect of HBAs. Initially, we studied the effect of HBAs on Kamlet–Taft parameters. Herein, the DESs were composed by ethylene glycol (EG) as the HBD and eight compounds as the HBAs with a molar ratio of HBD and HBA of 1:4. Besides, the influence of the anion type in HBAs on α, β, and π* was investigated. Four DESs, i.e., TMAC/EG—1:4, TMAA/EG—1:4, TBAC/EG—1:4, and TBAB/EG—1:4, were employed to discuss the relationship between the anion types of HBAs and the Kamlet–Taft parameters. As shown in Figure 3b, the α values of the four DESs were irregular and slightly different. Especially, the α value of TMAA/EG—1:4 was relatively low due to the higher basicity of acetate (Ac¯) than Cl¯. These results indicated that TMAA/EG—1:4 had the weakest hydrogen bond-donating ability among the four DESs. Moreover, the β value was mainly affected by the nature of the anion in the HBAs. TMAC/EG—1:4 has a larger β value than TMAA/EG—1:4. Generally, Cl¯ has a stronger ability to accept hydrogen atom than acetate (Ac¯), resulting from the fact that Cl¯ has a stronger ability to form hydrogen bonds than Ac¯. Thus, TMAC/EG—1:4 had a larger value of β. Meanwhile, for TBAC/EG—1:4 and TBAB/EG—1:4, the values of β were not much different, indicating that Cl¯ and Br¯ have similar proton-accepting ability. Additionally, the change on the value of π* followed a similar tendency with that for β value.

3.2.2. Effect of HBDs. Herein, 18 kinds of ChCl-based DESs were taken as the representative to discuss and analyze the effect of HBDs on the values of α, β, and π* (Figure 4). Similar to HBAs, the length of the alkyl chain in the HBDs also has strong impact on α, β, and π*. Three ChCl-polyalcohol [i.e., EG, 1,2-propylene glycol (PG), and 1,2-butanediol (BG)] DESs and three ChCl-acid [i.e., malonic acid (MA), succinic acid (SA), and glutaric acid (GluA)] DESs were employed to discuss the influence of alkyl chain length of HBDs. As shown in Figure 4a,b, the value of β was boosted by increasing the alkyl chain length of HBDs for both ChCl-polyalcohol or ChCl-acid DESs, resulting from the weakened cation–anion interaction with the increase of the alkyl chain, which was consistent with the previous reports that the hydrogen bond basicity of DESs depended on the alkyl chain length of the acid. 29,30 Moreover, the α value of ChCl-acid DESs were much larger than that of ChCl-polyalcohol DESs (Figure 4a,b), originating from the acidic nature of ChCl-acid DESs. 27 Besides, with the increase of the chain length of the organic acids, the α value of the DESs tended to decrease slightly, resulting from the fact that the acidity of the organic acids decreased with the increased alkyl chain length. /

Furthermore, the α, β, and π* of ChCl-based DESs (i.e., ChCl—polyalcohol DESs, ChCl—amide DESs, and ChCl—acid DESs) were discussed separately. First, we employed five alcohols as HBDs, including EG, PG, BG, glycerol (Gly), and benzyl alcohol (BA), at a ChCl/HBD molar ratio of 1:2. Obviously, the α value of the synthesized ChCl—polyalcohol DESs increased with the increasing number of hydroxyl groups in alcohols (Figure 4c) because more hydroxyl groups provided more sites to donate hydrogen bonds, and ChCl/ Gly—1:2 has the largest α value (0.93). Meanwhile, ChCl/ Gly—1:2 possesses the highest π* value (1.201) because more hydroxyl groups resulted in its high polarity and the strong ability to dipole–dipole and dipole-induced dipole inter- actions. In contrast, the β value (0.474) of ChCl/Gly—1:2 is the smallest, indicating its weakest ability to accept hydrogen. Additionally, the values of α, β, and π* for ChCl/BA—1:2 show a slight difference with other polyalcohol-based DESs owing to the electronic effect of benzene ring. Second, three

ChCl–amide DESs were prepared to employ urea, methyl urea, and acetamide as HBDs at a ChCl/HBD molar ratio of 1:2. Among these DESs (Figure 4d), ChCl/urea–1:2 has the highest α (0.992) and π* (1.218) values but the lowest β (0.447) value. Moreover, urea and methyl urea contained more –NH groups, resulting in the stronger hydrogen bond donating ability (higher α values) of ChCl/urea–1:2 and ChCl/methyl urea–1:2 than ChCl/acetamide–1:2. For ChCl/urea–1:2 and ChCl/methyl urea–1:2, the methyl group resulted in a decrease in the ability to donate hydrogens; thus, ChCl/methyl urea–1:2 has a lower α value (0.702). Besides, the methyl group also made ChCl/methyl urea–1:2 have a lower π* (1.111) value than ChCl/urea–1:2. Additionally, ChCl/urea–1:2 has the lowest β value (0.477). There was one hydroxyl (–OH) group in the choline cation, which would compete with cellulose to form a hydrogen bond with chlorine, resulting in poor solubility of cellulose (usually less than 1.0 wt %). For the dissolution of cellulose in ILs, the β and β–α values should be located within a certain section: 0.8 < β < 1.2 and 0.35 < β–α < 0.95, respectively. Owing to the greater β values (>0.8) of the investigated DESs, the DES should have relatively lower ability to donate hydrogen bonding in order to better dissolve cellulose. In other words, the DES with stronger basicity could potentially dissolve cellulose efficiently, which agreed with our previous results.⁹

Considering the low solubility of cellulose in the used DESs, the changes in cellulose after being dissolved and regenerated were not investigated in this work. However, Clough et al. have pointed out that it is not always an innocent dissolution process or reaction that could be expected, at least in some cases in ILs, 44 and so is the case of DESs. In the future, the influence of DESs on cellulose properties (i.e., molecular weight and crystalline allomorph) should be necessarily investigated for the designed new DESs of dissolving cellulose. Meanwhile, some types of DESs may lead to the formation of side products (e.g., 5-hydroxymethylfurfural), which also required more attention. ## 3.5. Effect of Different Interactions on the Correlation between Kamlet–Taft Parameters and Solubility. As discussed above, the dissolution ability of one DES was different for lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose, which was probably caused by the different mechanisms of the interaction between DES and different lignocellulosic components. First, lignin has plenty of intramolecular hydrogen bonding interactions and π···π stacking interactions. Breaking these two interactions is necessary to dissolve lignin in a solvent. Generally, two main non-covalent interactions, i.e., C–H···π and O···H bonding, could be formed between DESs and lignin. The formed interactions between DESs and lignin could efficiently destroy the intramolecular interactions of lignin owing to their greater interaction energy than that between lignin molecules, resulting in the successful dissolution of lignin in DESs. Although no π···π stacking interaction was generated between DESs and lignin, the strong O···H bonding can promote the dissolution of lignin in DESs.60 Second, the difficulty to dissolve cellulose and hemicellulose in conventional solvents originated from the intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonding interactions. Both HBDs and HBAs in DESs have sites to form hydrogen bonding interactions with the chains of cellulose and hemicellulose. Thus, during the dissolving of cellulose and hemicellulose in DESs, HBAs could form new hydrogen bonding with the –OH group and –CH2OH on cellulose and hemicellulose chains, while HBDs would form new hydrogen bonding with skeletal oxygen and –OH group on cellulose and hemicellulose chains. The synergistic effect of HBDs and HBAs leads to the destruction of the hydrogen bond network structure of cellulose and hemicellulose, thus resulting in the dissolution of cellulose and hemicellulose in DESs.61 From these discussions above, it could be observed that the interactions between DESs and lignin were complex, thus making the correlation between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the lignin solubility be unsatisfactory. In comparison, the interactions between DESs and cellulose/hemicellulose was only the hydrogen bonding interactions. Therefore, the solubility of cellulose/hemicellulose showed a good correlation with the β value for most of the developed DESs. It would be an interesting aspect to evaluate the correlation between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the solubility of the lignocellulosic components.

## 4. CONCLUSIONS Owing to their unique properties, DESs are up-and-coming alternatives to organic solvents, showing apparent advantages compared to ILs. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters can be used to characterize the properties of DESs. By analyzing the relationship between the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of 56 DESs, the following conclusions were drawn:

(1) The Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs were mainly related to the structures and properties of HBAs and HBDs. For example, the increase in the length of the alkyl chain would reduce the ability of the target substance to provide or accept hydrogen; thus, the

values of both α and β decreased with the increase in the alkyl chain length. The π* parameter was mainly related to the non-specific interaction between DESs and dyes. In addition, the water content significantly affected the Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs.

(2) Generally, DESs had relatively larger α and π* values but smaller β values than common molecular solvents. In comparison with ILs, DESs had larger α values, slightly smaller β and β−α (which could represent the net basicity of the solvents) values, and comparable π* values. As reported, ILs that could efficiently dissolve cellulose should have a β value ranging from 0.80 to 1.20, and the β−α (net basicity) value should not be less than 0.35 or more than 0.90. However, the developed DESs in this work also obey this rule to some extent. Although the investigated DESs had a β value of greater than 0.8, too weak net basicity (β−α < 0.35) resulted in the solubility of cellulose being very poor in these DESs. Notably, the solubility of lignin had a good linear correlation with the α−β (net acidity) values of the examined DESs, while the solubility of xylan well positively correlated with the β values of the determined DESs. However, the linear relationship between the solubility of lignin and xylan and other parameters was poor. In addition, although Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters can generally be a good indication for selecting DESs to dissolve cellulose, lignin, or hemi-cellulose efficiently, it sometimes did not necessarily mean that the DESs with suitable Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters certainly dissolved the three components of lignocellulose. Besides Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters, other factors, i.e., the properties of the components and other physicochemical properties, should also be considered when choosing the suitable DESs for dissolving lignocellulosic components. Therefore, caution should be kept on this point.

Therefore, by understanding the Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs, DESs could be reasonably designed as a suitable solvent for dissolving lignocellulose and its main components (i.e., cellulose, lignin, and hemicellulose). To fulfill this purpose, we are designing more types of DESs with diverse structures and properties, including those reported by other researchers, and are carefully determining their Kamlet–Taft parameters. By combining necessary theoretical calculations, we can obtain how the structures and properties of DESs intrinsically affect their Kamlet–Taft parameters. These developed DESs would be further applied to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. It is highly promising to reveal an accurate relationship between the solubility and Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs, which would guide the design of effective DESs to pretreat, dissolve, and even convert lignocellulose.

INTRODUCTION Lignocellulose, composed of three primary lignocellulosic components of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, is the largest renewable resource on earth. It can be used as an abundantly available raw material to produce value-added products, including transportation fuels, platform chemicals, and functional materials. 1,2 Generally, dissolution is indis- pensable to the efficient utilization or conversion of lignocellulose. Significant effort has been devoted to developing suitable solvents to dissolve lignocellulosic components, a research hotspot in the field of lignocellulose.3 Of the developed solvent systems, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been recognized as an emerging class of functional solvents for the dissolution of lignocellulosic components. Generally, DESs are composed of two components via the hydrogen bonding interaction to generate a eutectic mixture, and the two components are hydrogen- bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA), respectively. 4,5 The DESs designed by selecting suitable HBDs and HBAs of different properties could enable them to possess various unique advantages, e.g., strong solvation ability, good designability, low cost, facile preparation, high biocompati- bility, etc. 4-8 These characteristics of DESs promote the continually growing interest in constructing efficient DESs to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, or lignin.9-12 As reported, DESs can be defined as the mixture of two or more pure compounds with a eutectic point temperature below that for an ideal liquid mixture, showing significantly negative deviations from ideality. 13 More importantly, the composition of DESs should be in a certain range, not just in a fixed stoichiometric proportion. 13 Based on this definition, all the prepared solvents in this work can be considered as DESs. Regarding the utilization of DESs in lignocellulosic chemistry, the current attention is mainly focused on designing novel DESs for the pretreatment of lignocellulose or dissolution of the three major components. 14 Very little attention has been paid to system- atically analyze the relationship between the properties of DESs and the dissolution of lignocellulosic components, resulting in limited rules that can be followed to design or screen suitable DESs to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. 15 As is well known, whether a DES is a good solvent or not is mostly related to its solvation ability. Generally, the solvation properties of one specific solvent can be evaluated by Kamlet- Taft solvatochromic parameters (i.e., α, β, and π*), in which α represents the hydrogen-bond-donating ability (i.e., Lewis acidity), β represents the hydrogen-bond-accepting ability (i.e., Lewis basicity), and π* represents the polarizability of the solvents. Moreover, a positive linear relationship between α and the extraction efficiency of lignin was found when using different ChCl-based DESs to pretreat pine wood.¹⁹ In addition, our previous works showed that the solubility of lignin had a positive correlation with α and π* of the DESs, while the solubility of xylan had a positive correlation with β.¹¹,²⁰ However, previous works only investigated the relationship between Kamlet–Taft parameters of limited types of DESs and their performance on the pretreatment/dissolution of lignocellulose. More difficultly, although Kamlet–Taft parameters of some DESs have been experimentally determined or theoretically predicted,²¹ the reported parameters of DES are still highly limited compared with the great amount of DESs, let alone to numerous possible combinations of DESs which have not been investigated.²² Besides, the parameters reported in different works were not obtained by compatible methods, leading to the incomparability of these parameters. Owing to the insufficient and even incompatible data, Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters were still not the good indicators on the solute solubility in comparison with the surface tension and pKₐ. Therefore, it is a great challenge to evaluate the performance of DES on the dissolution of lignocellulosic components using the Kamlet–Taft parameters.²³ More effort should be devoted on investigating the correlation between the structures of DESs and Kamlet–Taft parameters and the relationship between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the solubility of lignocellulosic components. To better understand the Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs to facilitate the design of DESs to dissolve lignocellulosic components, 56 kinds of DESs were prepared using different HBAs and HBDs. Emphasizing, these DESs were selected based on the properties of HBAs and HBDs. Some previously reported DESs were directly selected, and most of the involved DESs were prepared based on our continuous jobs on the preparation of novel DESs to dissolve the lignocellulosic components. Initially, the influence of the structure (chain length) and properties of HBDs and HBAs on Kamlet–Taft parameters was analyzed. Additionally, the Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs were compared with those of conventional solvents and ionic liquids (ILs), providing a macroscopic image of Kamlet–Taft parameters of different solvents. Furthermore, the relationship between the Kamlet–Taft parameters of the DESs and the solubility of lignocellulosic 11724 https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.3c01309 Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2023, 62, 11723–11734 Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research pubs.acs.org/IECR Article components was investigated for better understanding the influence of DESs on the dissolution of lignocellulosic components. These results would help design robust DESs or simplify the selection process of DESs for dissolution of lignocellulosic components. Herein, we should point out that not all the used DESs were non-toxic by nature. The toxicity of DESs depends on the components used to form DESs. However, with the development of DESs, non-toxic and safe DESs, possessing the most suitable Kamlet–Taft parameters, could be constructed for dissolving lignocellulosic components. ## 2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION ### 3.1. Measurement of Kamlet–Taft Solvatochromic Parameters of DESs. The Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of the involved DESs (56 kinds, Scheme 1) were determined by the maximum UV–vis absorption peaks of the solutions of three dyes (Figure S1). The corresponding Kamlet–Taft parameters was the average of twice the measurements for each DES obtained from twice preparations (Table S2). Herein, it was emphasized that the Kamlet–Taft parameters of different solvents were determined using the same dyes (i.e., _N,N_-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4-nitroaniline, and Nile red) to exclude the influence of different dyes on the values of Kamlet–Taft parameters and make the results be comparable. By analyzing the values of α, β, and π*, we could conclude the relationship between the values of Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters and the structures and properties of DESs. Furthermore, by combining the solubility of cellulose, lignin, and hemicellulose in DESs, the correlation between solubility and Kamlet–Taft parameters could be revealed to some extent. 3.2. Comparison Kamlet–Taft Solvatochromic Parameters of DESs, ILs, and Molecular Solvents. For comparison, the Kamlet–Taft parameters of some common molecular solvents and ILs were collected from a typical literature³⁵ and are also provided in Tables S3 and S4. Considering that the Kamlet–Taft parameters of the prepared DESs were determined based on the reported method, the obtained results for the DESs were comparable with the data of common molecular solvents and ILs from the literature studies. It was found that water had larger α and π* values but a relatively smaller β value than most of other molecular solvents. However, there were great differences on the values of Kamlet–Taft parameters for water in different literature studies. More importantly, the synthesized DESs have relatively higher Kamlet–Taft parameters (α, β, and π*) than molecular solvents (Tables S2 and S3), which is consistent with the result that the α value of DESs is higher than that of most organic solvents predicted using the COSMO-RS model.36 Additionally, the Kamlet–Taft parameters of ILs are larger than those of molecular solvents (Tables S3 and S4), and protic ILs have larger α and β values than aprotic ILs, suggesting that protic ILs have stronger hydrogen bond-donating and hydrogen bond-accepting abilities. Effect of Different Interactions on the Correlation between Kamlet–Taft Parameters and Solubility. As discussed above, the dissolution ability of one DES was different for lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose, which was probably caused by the different mechanisms of the interaction between DES and different lignocellulosic components. First, lignin has plenty of intramolecular hydrogen bonding interactions and π···π stacking interactions. Breaking these two interactions is necessary to dissolve lignin in a solvent. Generally, two main non-covalent interactions, i.e., C–H···π and O···H bonding, could be formed between DESs and lignin. The formed interactions between DESs and lignin could efficiently destroy the intramolecular interactions of lignin owing to their greater interaction energy than that between lignin molecules, resulting in the successful dissolution of lignin in DESs. Although no π···π stacking interaction was generated between DESs and lignin, the strong O···H bonding can promote the dissolution of lignin in DESs.60 Second, the difficulty to dissolve cellulose and hemicellulose in conventional solvents originated from the intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonding interactions. Both HBDs and HBAs in DESs have sites to form hydrogen bonding interactions with the chains of cellulose and hemicellulose. Thus, during the dissolving of cellulose and hemicellulose in DESs, HBAs could form new hydrogen bonding with the –OH group and –CH2OH on cellulose and hemicellulose chains, while HBDs would form new hydrogen bonding with skeletal oxygen and –OH group on cellulose and hemicellulose chains. The synergistic effect of HBDs and HBAs leads to the destruction of the hydrogen bond network structure of cellulose and hemicellulose, thus resulting in the dissolution of cellulose and hemicellulose in DESs.61 From these discussions above, it could be observed that the interactions between DESs and lignin were complex, thus making the correlation between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the lignin solubility be unsatisfactory. In comparison, the interactions between DESs and cellulose/hemicellulose was only the hydrogen bonding interactions. Therefore, the solubility of cellulose/hemicellulose showed a good correlation with the β value for most of the developed DESs. It would be an interesting aspect to evaluate the correlation between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the solubility of the lignocellulosic components. ## 4. CONCLUSIONS Owing to their unique properties, DESs are up-and-coming alternatives to organic solvents, showing apparent advantages compared to ILs. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters can be used to characterize the properties of DESs. By analyzing the relationship between the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of 56 DESs, the following conclusions were drawn: (1) The Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs were mainly related to the structures and properties of HBAs and HBDs. For example, the increase in the length of the alkyl chain would reduce the ability of the target substance to provide or accept hydrogen; thus, the values of both α and β decreased with the increase in the alkyl chain length. The π* parameter was mainly related to the non-specific interaction between DESs and dyes. In addition, the water content significantly affected the Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs. (2) Generally, DESs had relatively larger α and π* values but smaller β values than common molecular solvents. In comparison with ILs, DESs had larger α values, slightly smaller β and β−α (which could represent the net basicity of the solvents) values, and comparable π* values. As reported, ILs that could efficiently dissolve cellulose should have a β value ranging from 0.80 to 1.20, and the β−α (net basicity) value should not be less than 0.35 or more than 0.90. However, the developed DESs in this work also obey this rule to some extent. Although the investigated DESs had a β value of greater than 0.8, too weak net basicity (β−α < 0.35) resulted in the solubility of cellulose being very poor in these DESs. Notably, the solubility of lignin had a good linear correlation with the α−β (net acidity) values of the examined DESs, while the solubility of xylan well positively correlated with the β values of the determined DESs. However, the linear relationship between the solubility of lignin and xylan and other parameters was poor. In addition, although Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters can generally be a good indication for selecting DESs to dissolve cellulose, lignin, or hemi-cellulose efficiently, it sometimes did not necessarily mean that the DESs with suitable Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters certainly dissolved the three components of lignocellulose. Besides Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters, other factors, i.e., the properties of the components and other physicochemical properties, should also be considered when choosing the suitable DESs for dissolving lignocellulosic components. Therefore, caution should be kept on this point. Therefore, by understanding the Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs, DESs could be reasonably designed as a suitable solvent for dissolving lignocellulose and its main components (i.e., cellulose, lignin, and hemicellulose). To fulfill this purpose, we are designing more types of DESs with diverse structures and properties, including those reported by other researchers, and are carefully determining their Kamlet–Taft parameters. By combining necessary theoretical calculations, we can obtain how the structures and properties of DESs intrinsically affect their Kamlet–Taft parameters. These developed DESs would be further applied to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. It is highly promising to reveal an accurate relationship between the solubility and Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs, which would guide the design of effective DESs to pretreat, dissolve, and even convert lignocellulose. INTRODUCTION Lignocellulose, composed of three primary lignocellulosic components of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, is the largest renewable resource on earth. It can be used as an abundantly available raw material to produce value-added products, including transportation fuels, platform chemicals, and functional materials. 1,2 Generally, dissolution is indis- pensable to the efficient utilization or conversion of lignocellulose. Significant effort has been devoted to developing suitable solvents to dissolve lignocellulosic components, a research hotspot in the field of lignocellulose.3 Of the developed solvent systems, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been recognized as an emerging class of functional solvents for the dissolution of lignocellulosic components. Generally, DESs are composed of two components via the hydrogen bonding interaction to generate a eutectic mixture, and the two components are hydrogen- bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen-bond acceptor (HBA), respectively. 4,5 The DESs designed by selecting suitable HBDs and HBAs of different properties could enable them to possess various unique advantages, e.g., strong solvation ability, good designability, low cost, facile preparation, high biocompati- bility, etc. 4-8 These characteristics of DESs promote the continually growing interest in constructing efficient DESs to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, or lignin.9-12 As reported, DESs can be defined as the mixture of two or more pure compounds with a eutectic point temperature below that for an ideal liquid mixture, showing significantly negative deviations from ideality. 13 More importantly, the composition of DESs should be in a certain range, not just in a fixed stoichiometric proportion. 13 Based on this definition, all the prepared solvents in this work can be considered as DESs. Regarding the utilization of DESs in lignocellulosic chemistry, the current attention is mainly focused on designing novel DESs for the pretreatment of lignocellulose or dissolution of the three major components. 14 Very little attention has been paid to system- atically analyze the relationship between the properties of DESs and the dissolution of lignocellulosic components, resulting in limited rules that can be followed to design or screen suitable DESs to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. 15 As is well known, whether a DES is a good solvent or not is mostly related to its solvation ability. Generally, the solvation properties of one specific solvent can be evaluated by Kamlet- Taft solvatochromic parameters (i.e., α, β, and π*), in which α represents the hydrogen-bond-donating ability (i.e., Lewis acidity), β represents the hydrogen-bond-accepting ability (i.e., Lewis basicity), and π* represents the polarizability of the solvents. Effect of Different Interactions on the Correlation between Kamlet–Taft Parameters and Solubility. As discussed above, the dissolution ability of one DES was different for lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose, which was probably caused by the different mechanisms of the interaction between DES and different lignocellulosic components. First, lignin has plenty of intramolecular hydrogen bonding interactions and π···π stacking interactions. Breaking these two interactions is necessary to dissolve lignin in a solvent. Generally, two main non-covalent interactions, i.e., C–H···π and O···H bonding, could be formed between DESs and lignin. The formed interactions between DESs and lignin could efficiently destroy the intramolecular interactions of lignin owing to their greater interaction energy than that between lignin molecules, resulting in the successful dissolution of lignin in DESs. Although no π···π stacking interaction was generated between DESs and lignin, the strong O···H bonding can promote the dissolution of lignin in DESs.60 Second, the difficulty to dissolve cellulose and hemicellulose in conventional solvents originated from the intramolecular and intermolecular hydrogen bonding interactions. Both HBDs and HBAs in DESs have sites to form hydrogen bonding interactions with the chains of cellulose and hemicellulose. Thus, during the dissolving of cellulose and hemicellulose in DESs, HBAs could form new hydrogen bonding with the –OH group and –CH2OH on cellulose and hemicellulose chains, while HBDs would form new hydrogen bonding with skeletal oxygen and –OH group on cellulose and hemicellulose chains. The synergistic effect of HBDs and HBAs leads to the destruction of the hydrogen bond network structure of cellulose and hemicellulose, thus resulting in the dissolution of cellulose and hemicellulose in DESs.61 From these discussions above, it could be observed that the interactions between DESs and lignin were complex, thus making the correlation between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the lignin solubility be unsatisfactory. In comparison, the interactions between DESs and cellulose/hemicellulose was only the hydrogen bonding interactions. Therefore, the solubility of cellulose/hemicellulose showed a good correlation with the β value for most of the developed DESs. It would be an interesting aspect to evaluate the correlation between Kamlet–Taft parameters and the solubility of the lignocellulosic components. ## 4. CONCLUSIONS Owing to their unique properties, DESs are up-and-coming alternatives to organic solvents, showing apparent advantages compared to ILs. The Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters can be used to characterize the properties of DESs. By analyzing the relationship between the Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of 56 DESs, the following conclusions were drawn: (1) The Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs were mainly related to the structures and properties of HBAs and HBDs. For example, the increase in the length of the alkyl chain would reduce the ability of the target substance to provide or accept hydrogen; thus, the values of both α and β decreased with the increase in the alkyl chain length. The π* parameter was mainly related to the non-specific interaction between DESs and dyes. In addition, the water content significantly affected the Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs. (2) Generally, DESs had relatively larger α and π* values but smaller β values than common molecular solvents. In comparison with ILs, DESs had larger α values, slightly smaller β and β−α (which could represent the net basicity of the solvents) values, and comparable π* values. As reported, ILs that could efficiently dissolve cellulose should have a β value ranging from 0.80 to 1.20, and the β−α (net basicity) value should not be less than 0.35 or more than 0.90. However, the developed DESs in this work also obey this rule to some extent. Although the investigated DESs had a β value of greater than 0.8, too weak net basicity (β−α < 0.35) resulted in the solubility of cellulose being very poor in these DESs. Notably, the solubility of lignin had a good linear correlation with the α−β (net acidity) values of the examined DESs, while the solubility of xylan well positively correlated with the β values of the determined DESs. However, the linear relationship between the solubility of lignin and xylan and other parameters was poor. In addition, although Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters can generally be a good indication for selecting DESs to dissolve cellulose, lignin, or hemi-cellulose efficiently, it sometimes did not necessarily mean that the DESs with suitable Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters certainly dissolved the three components of lignocellulose. Besides Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters, other factors, i.e., the properties of the components and other physicochemical properties, should also be considered when choosing the suitable DESs for dissolving lignocellulosic components. Therefore, caution should be kept on this point. Therefore, by understanding the Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs, DESs could be reasonably designed as a suitable solvent for dissolving lignocellulose and its main components (i.e., cellulose, lignin, and hemicellulose). To fulfill this purpose, we are designing more types of DESs with diverse structures and properties, including those reported by other researchers, and are carefully determining their Kamlet–Taft parameters. By combining necessary theoretical calculations, we can obtain how the structures and properties of DESs intrinsically affect their Kamlet–Taft parameters. These developed DESs would be further applied to dissolve cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. It is highly promising to reveal an accurate relationship between the solubility and Kamlet–Taft parameters of DESs, which would guide the design of effective DESs to pretreat, dissolve, and even convert lignocellulose.
